leviathan

luh-VY-uh-thun · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Leviathan is something enormous and extremely powerful, especially an organization, vehicle, or creature.

The new aircraft carrier was a true leviathan, longer than three football fields and carrying over five thousand crew members.

Example

Critics described the merged corporation as a leviathan capable of crushing any small competitor that dared challenge it.

Leviathan is used for something so massive and powerful that it feels almost impossible to resist or compete with.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

giant: A giant is anything remarkably big of its kind -- a giant pumpkin, a retail giant. The word measures size and little else. A leviathan is enormous and mighty at once: so vast and powerful that resisting it feels hopeless.

behemoth: A behemoth is something huge and hulking -- the word leans on sheer bulk, often with a hint of lumbering clumsiness. A leviathan pairs its vast size with power and menace: the monster of the deep, not merely the biggest thing in the room.

juggernaut: A juggernaut is a force that cannot be stopped once it is moving -- its whole point is crushing momentum, not bulk. A leviathan is defined by enormous size and power, and it can loom over everything while sitting perfectly still.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

midget: something very small

trifle: something of very little importance or size

Where it sits · how overwhelming the size is — large → leviathan → colossal

large vs. leviathan: Large is a plain, everyday word for size, without leviathan's sense of overwhelming, almost intimidating scale.

colossal vs. leviathan: Colossal goes beyond even a leviathan in sheer scale, describing something so gigantic it hardly seems possible at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

origin — livyathan

origin — livyathan: a giant sea monster (Hebrew livyathan, from the Bible)

Put it together

Put it together: Leviathan comes from Hebrew livyathan, the name of a monstrous sea creature described in the Bible -- so massive and powerful that its name eventually came to describe any enormous, overwhelming thing.

Use the root in a new word: Leviathan (the book)

Use the root in a new word: Leviathan (the book): In 1651, philosopher Thomas Hobbes named his famous book about government Leviathan, comparing a powerful state to the biblical sea monster -- huge, and impossible to fight alone.
